newsitem.title: USA: Victims' families hope McVeigh's ideas die with him.
newsitem.headline: Victims' families hope McVeigh's ideas die with him.

text.p: The families of Timothy McVeigh's bomb victims applauded the death sentence handed down against him on Friday and said they hoped the anti-government paranoia that inspired the attack would die with him.

Dozens of people gathered at the downtown Oklahoma City site where the blast on April 19, 1995 killed 168 people, and many applauded briefly as news came through that McVeigh had been sentenced to death inside a courtroom 600 miles (1,000 km) away in Denver.
There was, however, much less joy at the bombing site than when the Denver jury found McVeigh guilty on all charges against him last week.

"You don't want to celebrate somebody else's death," said Catherine Alaniz, whose father Claude Medearis was killed in the blast. "But my dad didn't have a choice to live or die and I don't think McVeigh should either. We got the verdict that we deserved."
The vast majority of survivors and the relatives of those killed had called for the death penalty.

"The punishment fits the crime. I mean, he killed 168 people. What other sentence could there be?" said Jim Denny, whose young son suffered brain damage in the bombing and whose daughter was also injured.

Behind him, a small group of victims sang "God Bless America" as they hung an American flag on the chain-link fence that surrounds the grassy field where the Alfred P. Murrah federal building stood before it was torn apart by McVeigh's truck bomb.
McVeigh was a decorated Gulf War veteran whose anti- government ideas turned to violence after 82 Branch Davidian cult members were killed in a siege by federal agents at Waco, Texas.
He bombed the Murrah building on the second anniversary of the fiery end to the Waco siege, allegedly hoping his terrorist attack would spark an uprising against the federal government.
The families of those killed said they hoped the death sentence would send a message to right-wing extremists like McVeigh that Americans will not tolerate their message of violence.

"If he were to let him off with a light sentence, who knows how many other people would want to step up to the plate and do the same thing?" said Kathleen Treanor, whose four-year-old daughter Ashley Eckles was killed. "We have to make sure this doesn't happen again and if we had backed away from the death penalty issue, it would encourage other radicals out there."
Calvin Mosier, who was injured in the bombing and lost a close friend, said any other sentence would have allowed McVeigh to promote his cause from inside prison.
"He'll not be able to espouse his theories and ideas on a network or computer. His story is ended," Mosier said.
